C0.quote: a voting rule aggregates this data into the final outcome
C0.note: Paper studies statistical cultures for sampling approval elections and maps of elections; borderline but about approval voting elections and ABC rules, so coded eligible.

C1.quote: Computing the isomorphic Hamming distance between two approval elections is NP-hard.
C1.note: Mainly simulations on synthetic (and some real PB) data; one NP-hardness result and a sampling proposition. EM-like Pabulib data is only a comparison dataset.

C2.1.quote: Each voter v ∈ V casts an approval ballot

C2.2.quote: he or she selects a subset of candidates that he or she approves

C2.3.note: Voters' approval ballots are the only objects; no separate held attitudes. Euclidean model uses points to generate ballots, but these are generative models rather than modelled voter attitudes.

C2.4.quote: Each voter v ∈ V casts an approval ballot
C2.4.note: Input described only as a submitted ballot; C2.3 = N.

C4.1.note: No utility/welfare/satisfaction notions for voters are used in the formal sense. Voter-satisfaction-like notions appear only via cohesiveness and proportionality.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' appears only in a reference title (Elkind and Lackner).

C5.1.quote: Fraction of voters that belong to at least one 1-cohesive group
C5.1.note: Cohesiveness level and voters in cohesive groups are statistics related to proportional representation (justified representation) that are computed in the experiments.

C5.2.quote: Fraction of voters that belong to at least one 1-cohesive group
C5.2.note: Computed on approval ballots, with no statement relating them to held attitudes.

C9.1.note: Claims concern which models to use in experiments and what matters for rules; conclusion proposes a baseline model for numerical experiments.

C9.2.note: The claims follow from the experimental results on ballots; no hidden assumptions about held attitudes, strategy, or information are needed. This is a weak determination.
